statements.statement:
For every finite \(m\geq1\) and every \(0<\epsilon<1/2\), let \(d_m(\epsilon)\) be the uniform approximation modulus in the preceding definition.  Put \(\rho=1-2\epsilon\) and
\[
 E_m(\epsilon)=\frac{1}{T_m(1/\rho)}
 =\operatorname{sech}\!\left(m\operatorname{arcosh}(1/\rho)\right),
\]
where \(T_m\) is the degree-\(m\) Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind.  Then
\[
 \max_{b\in\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon}}\{U_m(b)-L_m(b)\}
 =\sup_{b\in\operatorname{relint}(\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon})}\{U_m(b)-L_m(b)\}
 =2d_m(\epsilon),
\]
and
\[
 0<d_m(\epsilon)\leq E_m(\epsilon)\leq\rho^m.
\]
Moreover, \(E_m(\epsilon)<\rho^m\) whenever \(m\geq2\).  Consequently every feasible fiber has width at most
\[
 2\operatorname{sech}\!\left(m\operatorname{arcosh}\!\left(\frac{1}{1-2\epsilon}\right)\right).
\]
For every \(0<\delta\leq2\), the integer plate-size condition
\[
 m\geq
 \frac{\operatorname{arcosh}(2/\delta)}
 {\operatorname{arcosh}(1/(1-2\epsilon))}
\]
guarantees \(U_m(b)-L_m(b)\leq\delta\) simultaneously for all \(b\in\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon}\).
statements.justification: The theorem identifies the exact worst-case width as twice a best-approximation modulus and gives a shifted-Chebyshev hyperbolic-secant upper bound, while retaining strict nonidentification for every finite plate size.
statements.gap: Fixed-plate mixture nonidentification results do not identify the exact uniform width as a best-approximation modulus or provide this explicit shifted-Chebyshev plate-size guarantee for the nonlinear causal functional.
statements.consumer: For \(0<\delta\leq2\), a design analyst may choose \(m\geq\operatorname{arcosh}(2/\delta)/\operatorname{arcosh}(1/(1-2\epsilon))\) to cap worst-case latent-mixture identification width by \(\delta\); this is not a sampling-error rate in \(n\) or a CAD runtime claim.
statements.proof_tex:
Write \(K=K_{\epsilon}\), \(V=V_m\), and \(d=d_m(\epsilon)\).  The overlap restriction gives \(p(q)\in[\epsilon,1-\epsilon]\), so the denominators in \(f\) are positive on \(K\).  Hence \(f\in C(K)\), because \(K\) is compact and the cell-coordinate maps are continuous.  The multinomial identity gives
\[
 \sum_{c\in\mathcal I_m}B_c^{(m)}(q)
 =\left(\sum_{a,y}q_{ay}\right)^m=1,
\]
so \(1\in V\).

First fix \(b\in\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon}\) and \(\nu_1,\nu_0\in\mathcal F_{m,\epsilon}(b)\).  The signed measure \(\zeta=\nu_1-\nu_0\) satisfies, by the defining moment constraints,
\[
 \int_K B_c^{(m)}\,d\zeta=0
 \qquad(c\in\mathcal I_m).
\]
Consequently \(\int_Kv\,d\zeta=0\) for every \(v\in V\).  Because \(\nu_1\) and \(\nu_0\) are probability measures, \(\lVert\zeta\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\leq2\).  Thus every \(v\in V\) obeys
\[
 \left|\int_K f\,d\nu_1-\int_K f\,d\nu_0\right|
 =\left|\int_K(f-v)\,d\zeta\right|
 \leq2\lVert f-v\rVert_{\infty,K}.
\]
Taking the infimum over \(v\in V\) and then the supremum over ordered pairs in the nonempty fiber yields
\[
 U_m(b)-L_m(b)\leq2d. \tag{1}
\]
Here \(\sup S-\inf S=\sup_{s_1,s_0\in S}(s_1-s_0)\) for every nonempty bounded \(S\subset\mathbb R\), so endpoint attainment is not being assumed.

We next show that equality in (1) occurs for some feasible moment vector.  The space \(V\) is finite dimensional and therefore closed in \(C(K)\).  By \(\texttt{lem:finite-plate-nonpolynomial}\), \(f\notin V\), and hence \(d>0\).  Applying \(\texttt{lem:hahn-banach-quotient-norm}\) to \(C(K)\), \(V\), and \(f\) gives \(\Lambda\in C(K)^*\) such that
\[
 \lVert\Lambda\rVert=1,
 \qquad \Lambda(v)=0\quad(v\in V),
 \qquad \Lambda(f)=d. \tag{2}
\]
By \(\texttt{lem:riesz-markov-representation}\) and \(\texttt{lem:jordan-decomposition-signed-measure}\), there are mutually singular finite positive measures \(\sigma^+\) and \(\sigma^-\) on \(K\) such that \(\sigma=\sigma^+-\sigma^-\),
\[
 \Lambda(h)=\int_Kh\,d\sigma
 \quad(h\in C(K)),
 \qquad
 \sigma^+(K)+\sigma^-(K)=|\sigma|(K)=1. \tag{3}
\]
Since \(1\in V\), equations (2)--(3) imply
\[
 0=\Lambda(1)=\sigma^+(K)-\sigma^-(K).
\]
Together with (3), this gives \(\sigma^+(K)=\sigma^-(K)=1/2\).  Therefore \(\nu_+=2\sigma^+\) and \(\nu_-=2\sigma^-\) are probability measures on \(K\).  For every \(c\in\mathcal I_m\), equation (2) gives
\[
 \int_KB_c^{(m)}\,d\nu_+
 -\int_KB_c^{(m)}\,d\nu_-
 =2\Lambda(B_c^{(m)})=0.
\]
Thus \(\nu_+\) and \(\nu_-\) have a common moment vector \(b_*\in\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon}\), whereas
\[
 \int_Kf\,d\nu_+-\int_Kf\,d\nu_-
 =2\Lambda(f)=2d. \tag{4}
\]
Combining (1) and (4) proves
\[
 \max_{b\in\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon}}
 \{U_m(b)-L_m(b)\}=2d. \tag{5}
\]

For completeness, the relative interior of the moment body is nonempty without any extra support assumption.  If its affine dimension is \(r\), choose affinely independent \(z_0,\ldots,z_r\in\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon}\) whose affine hull is \(\operatorname{aff}(\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon})\).  The barycenter \(b_0=(r+1)^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^rz_j\) has a relative open ball contained in the simplex \(\operatorname{conv}\{z_0,\ldots,z_r\}\), hence \(b_0\in\operatorname{relint}(\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon})\).  By \(\texttt{def:bernstein-moment-body}\), choose \(\eta\in\mathcal F_{m,\epsilon}(b_0)\).  For \(0\leq t<1\), define
\[
 \nu_{t,+}=(1-t)\eta+t\nu_+,
 \qquad
 \nu_{t,-}=(1-t)\eta+t\nu_-,
 \qquad
 b_t=(1-t)b_0+tb_*.
\]
Linearity of all Bernstein moments puts both measures in \(\mathcal F_{m,\epsilon}(b_t)\).  If the relative ball of radius \(r_0>0\) about \(b_0\) lies in \(\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon}\), then the relative ball of radius \((1-t)r_0\) about \(b_t\) also lies there: each of its points has the form \((1-t)(b_0+h)+tb_*\) with \(\lVert h\rVert<r_0\), and convexity applies.  Hence \(b_t\in\operatorname{relint}(\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon})\).  Equation (4) now gives
\[
 U_m(b_t)-L_m(b_t)
 \geq\int_Kf\,d\nu_{t,+}-\int_Kf\,d\nu_{t,-}
 =2td.
\]
Letting \(t\uparrow1\) and using (1) proves
\[
 \sup_{b\in\operatorname{relint}(\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon})}
 \{U_m(b)-L_m(b)\}=2d. \tag{6}
\]

It remains to establish the constructive Chebyshev bound.  Define the Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind by
\[
 T_0(x)=1,\qquad T_1(x)=x,
 \qquad T_{k+1}(x)=2xT_k(x)-T_{k-1}(x).
\]
Induction in this recurrence shows that \(T_m\) is a polynomial of degree \(m\) and that
\[
 T_m(-x)=(-1)^mT_m(x). \tag{7}
\]
The angle-addition identities, followed by induction in the same recurrence, give
\[
 T_m(\cos\theta)=\cos(m\theta),
 \qquad
 T_m(\cosh a)=\cosh(ma). \tag{8}
\]
The first identity in (8) implies \(|T_m(x)|\leq1\) for \(|x|\leq1\).

Put \(\rho=1-2\epsilon\in(0,1)\) and define the degree-\(m\) polynomial
\[
 R_m(p)=(-1)^m
 \frac{T_m((2p-1)/\rho)}{T_m(1/\rho)}. \tag{9}
\]
The denominator in (9) is positive: for
\[
 a=\operatorname{arcosh}(1/\rho)>0,
\]
the second identity in (8) gives \(T_m(1/\rho)=\cosh(ma)>0\).  By (7),
\[
 R_m(0)=(-1)^m\frac{T_m(-1/\rho)}{T_m(1/\rho)}=1, \tag{10}
\]
and, again by (7),
\[
 R_m(1-p)=(-1)^mR_m(p). \tag{11}
\]
For \(p\in[\epsilon,1-\epsilon]\), one has \(|(2p-1)/\rho|\leq1\).  Therefore (8)--(9) imply
\[
 |R_m(p)|\leq \frac{1}{T_m(1/\rho)}
 =\operatorname{sech}(ma)=E_m(\epsilon). \tag{12}
\]

Because \(R_m\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(m\) and (10) says that \(1-R_m\) vanishes at zero, the polynomial factor theorem gives a polynomial
\[
 P_{m-1}(p)=\frac{1-R_m(p)}{p} \tag{13}
\]
of degree at most \(m-1\).  On \(K\), set
\[
 y_1=\frac{q_{11}}{p(q)},
 \qquad
 y_0=\frac{q_{01}}{1-p(q)}.
\]
The overlap inequalities make both divisions valid.  Moreover,
\[
 0\leq y_1\leq1,
 \qquad
 0\leq y_0\leq1, \tag{14}
\]
because \(q_{11}\leq p(q)\) and \(q_{01}\leq1-p(q)\).  With \(p=p(q)\), define
\[
 v_m(q)=q_{11}P_{m-1}(p)-q_{01}P_{m-1}(1-p)
 +\mathbf 1_{\{m\ {\rm odd}\}}R_m(p). \tag{15}
\]
Each of the first two terms in (15) is a cell coordinate multiplied by a polynomial of degree at most \(m-1\) in the linear polynomial \(p\), and the last term has degree at most \(m\).  Thus \(v_m\) is the restriction to the simplex of a polynomial of total degree at most \(m\).  By \(\texttt{lem:finite-plate-nonpolynomial}\), whose first assertion identifies the degree-\(m\) polynomial restrictions with \(V_m\), we have \(v_m\in V_m\).

Equations (11), (13), and (15), together with \(q_{11}=py_1\), \(q_{01}=(1-p)y_0\), and \(f=y_1-y_0\), yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
 f(q)-v_m(q)
 &=R_m(p)y_1-R_m(1-p)y_0
   -\mathbf 1_{\{m\ {\rm odd}\}}R_m(p)\\
 &=
 \begin{cases}
 R_m(p)(y_1-y_0),&m\text{ even},\\
 R_m(p)(y_1+y_0-1),&m\text{ odd}.
 \end{cases}
\end{aligned} \tag{16}
\]
Both brackets in (16) have absolute value at most one by (14).  Hence (12) and \(v_m\in V_m\) show
\[
 d_m(\epsilon)
 \leq\lVert f-v_m\rVert_{\infty,K}
 \leq E_m(\epsilon). \tag{17}
\]

The hyperbolic formula and its comparison with the geometric bound are elementary consequences of (8).  Since \(\cosh a=1/\rho\),
\[
 E_m(\epsilon)=\frac{1}{T_m(1/\rho)}
 =\frac{1}{\cosh(ma)}=\operatorname{sech}(ma). \tag{18}
\]
For \(m=1\), (18) gives \(E_1(\epsilon)=\rho\).  For every integer \(m\geq2\), the function \(x\mapsto x^m\) has positive second derivative on \((0,\infty)\); strict midpoint convexity and \(e^a\ne e^{-a}\) therefore give
\[
 \cosh(ma)=\frac{e^{ma}+e^{-ma}}{2}
 >\left(\frac{e^a+e^{-a}}{2}\right)^m
 =\cosh^m(a).
\]
Taking positive reciprocals yields
\[
 0<E_m(\epsilon)<\operatorname{sech}^m(a)=\rho^m
 \qquad(m\geq2), \tag{19}
\]
while equality holds in the comparison when \(m=1\).  Equations (17), (19), and \(d>0\) prove
\[
 0<d_m(\epsilon)\leq E_m(\epsilon)\leq\rho^m,
\]
with the asserted strict second inequality for \(m\geq2\).  Combining (1) and (17) gives the claimed uniform width bound \(2\operatorname{sech}(ma)\).

Finally, let \(0<\delta\leq2\).  Then \(\operatorname{arcosh}(2/\delta)\) is defined and nonnegative.  If
\[
 m\geq\frac{\operatorname{arcosh}(2/\delta)}{a},
\]
then \(ma\geq\operatorname{arcosh}(2/\delta)\).  Since \(\cosh\) is increasing on \([0,\infty)\),
\[
 \cosh(ma)\geq\frac{2}{\delta},
 \qquad
 2E_m(\epsilon)=\frac{2}{\cosh(ma)}\leq\delta.
\]
Together with (1) and (17), this proves \(U_m(b)-L_m(b)\leq\delta\) for every \(b\in\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon}\).  The argument establishes a uniform identification-width bound in the plate size \(m\); it asserts neither \(d_m(\epsilon)=E_m(\epsilon)\) nor an exact asymptotic formula.

sampling_model.design: Observational hierarchical sampling with a fixed plate of \(m\) individuals per cluster.
sampling_model.units: The \(n\) clusters are independent draws; conditional on \(Q_i\), the \(m\) individual causal vectors are iid.
sampling_model.treatment: Treatment is binary and conditionally ignorable given \(Q_i\); because \(Q_i\in K_{\epsilon}\), its cluster-specific probability \(p(Q_i)\) lies in \([\epsilon,1-\epsilon]\).
sampling_model.observed_data: Only \(C_i\), the four-cell multinomial count of \((A,Y)\) within cluster \(i\), is observed.
sampling_model.latent_structure: Every class member contains \(\mu\in\mathcal P(K_{\epsilon})\), draws \(Q_i\sim\mu\), and satisfies \(\Pr((A_{ij},Y_{ij})=(a,y)\mid Q_i)=Q_{i,ay}\) almost surely for every cell and individual.
sampling_model.overlap: Overlap is encoded by the declared spaces \(\mu\in\mathcal P(K_{\epsilon})\) and \(Q_i\in K_{\epsilon}\), not by a separate support assumption.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: The finite-dimensional observable nuisance is the multinomial count law \(b\), estimated by \(\widehat b\); the mixing law is not estimated pointwise.

estimand_functional: \(\Theta_{m,\epsilon}(b)=[L_m(b),U_m(b)]\) for every \(b\in\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon}\); if \(b\in\operatorname{relint}(\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon})\), this interval also equals \(\left[\max_{\lambda:\sum_c\lambda_cB_c^{(m)}\leq f}\lambda^\top b,\min_{\lambda:\sum_c\lambda_cB_c^{(m)}\geq f}\lambda^\top b\right]\), with both extrema attained. For \(d_m(\epsilon)\) as explicitly defined in Definition \texttt{def:uniform-identification-modulus}, \(\max_{b\in\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon}}\{U_m(b)-L_m(b)\}=\sup_{b\in\operatorname{relint}(\mathcal B_{m,\epsilon})}\{U_m(b)-L_m(b)\}=2d_m(\epsilon)\). Writing \(\rho=1-2\epsilon\), the shifted-Chebyshev construction gives \(0<d_m(\epsilon)\leq\operatorname{sech}(m\operatorname{arcosh}(1/\rho))\leq\rho^m\), with the last inequality strict for \(m\geq2\). Thus every feasible width is at most \(2\operatorname{sech}(m\operatorname{arcosh}(1/(1-2\epsilon)))\), without claiming equality between the modulus and this upper bound or an exact asymptotic.

tldr: Fixed-size cluster counts reveal only degree-\(m\) Bernstein moments of latent four-cell exposure--outcome laws, so the cluster-equally-weighted ATE is an interval rather than a point. Each hierarchical SCM carries \(\mu\in\mathcal P(K_{\epsilon})\), draws \(Q_i\sim\mu\), and calibrates the observed four-cell law to \(Q_i\). The sharp interval has attained measure and Bernstein-polynomial programs for every relative-interior count law, with compatible endpoint SCMs using at most \({m+3\choose3}\) latent laws. A generic contact-hull theorem exactly characterizes equality with any valid degree-\(m\) count-measurable envelope and gives strict improvement regions, while exact multinomial likelihood inversion produces a semialgebraic ATE confidence set recoverable by terminating CAD.

project_justification.gap: The São Paulo DOT analysis shows that city random-effect choices move the posterior ATE, while fixed-plate mixture theory establishes finite-moment information loss without characterizing this causal functional. Existing limited-pooling ATE bounds use particular valid polynomials, and generalized-moment theory lacks the hierarchical SCM semantics and strict-fiber conclusion.
project_justification.niche: The observable cluster-count law is finite dimensional, but the latent city law is unrestricted and the causal target is a nonlinear reciprocal functional. This creates a tractable convex moment geometry whose causal identified set has not been characterized.
project_justification.fill: The paper derives the sharp primal--dual interval, proves an iff Bernstein-span identification frontier and strict width throughout the relative interior, constructs finite-latent endpoint SCMs, gives an exact contact-hull criterion and strict improvement regions for every valid degree-\(m\) envelope with Lee--Weidner as a corollary, and turns exact multinomial inversion into a one-dimensional semialgebraic confidence set with terminating CAD recovery.

related_work: Nobre, Schmidt, Moodie, and Stephens (2023, Sections 5--6 and Figure 3) motivate the problem by documenting ATE sensitivity to city random effects in the São Paulo DOT study. Wood (1999, Introduction and Sections 2--4, especially Example 2 on pp. 1717--1718) develops fixed-binomial convex geometry and exhibits a polygonal nonidentifiable slice but does not study a four-cell causal functional. Wood (1992, p. 1167) connects binomial-mixture membership to infinite extendibility of a finite exchangeable Bernoulli law; this is background for the repeated-observation interpretation, not a causal-functional comparator. Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983) provide the standard conditional-ignorability framework and Rubin (1974) the potential-outcome framework underlying consistency; here ignorability is imposed conditional on latent \(Q_i\), and these assumptions are used in lem:scm-moment-reduction to map calibrated observed cells to the causal integrand. Lee and Weidner (2026, Section 4.2 and Proposition 2) are provenance only for the explicitly defined scalar-reference, count-law-only transplant, whose validity is proved directly from the displayed formulas; Section 5 and Theorem 3 give their associated fixed-order sample construction and asymptotic inference. This is not a comparison with their full covariate-dependent procedure. Bertsimas and Popescu (2005, Theorem 2.2) and Halaseh, Magron, and Skomra (2026, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 5.9) inform the strong-duality and full-support arguments. Bayer and Teichmann (2006, Theorem 1) inform atomic compression, while the endpoint contact face yields the causal support cap. Sachs, Jonzon, Sjölander, and Gabriel (2023, Sections 2--4) derive tight symbolic bounds by linear programming and vertex enumeration for categorical causal DAGs after reducing latent influences to a finite response-function state space, with linear observed-probability constraints and a linear causal query. They do not treat an unrestricted Borel mixing law over a continuous four-cell simplex, Bernstein moment fibers with the rational ATE functional, the required finite-atom reduction, or CAD recovery of an exact-inversion confidence set. Duarte et al. (2023, Proposition 1 and Algorithm 1) compute numerical polynomial causal bounds for finite discrete SCMs; the present continuous-latent problem first requires endpoint compression and then exact quantifier elimination. England, Bradford, and Davenport (2020, Theorem 1 and Algorithm 1) supply the CAD machinery. Bugni (2010, Theorems 1--3) motivates whole-set coverage, while Basu, Brill, and Yekutieli (2026, Section 4) motivate exact finite-sample inversion; neither source proves that the inverted hierarchical ATE set is semialgebraic or CAD-recoverable.
technical_internal_limitation: The exact \(m=2\) presolve certificate remains outstanding. For the rational full-support benchmark \(b_2^*\), finite-grid primal and dual linear programs agree numerically at approximately \([-0.05998,0.05998]\) and use ten active atoms, but this is not an algebraic CAD certificate and is not evidence for the exact endpoint values. The proposal therefore retains exact \(m=2\) primal--dual recovery as part of the open boundary-atlas question and as a required implementation kill test.
honest_scope: The central identification theorems concern relative-interior count laws and fixed finite \(m\). The Dirac-fiber proposition records point-identified boundary images for \(m\ge2\), so strict width is not asserted on the boundary. Whole-set coverage is only the immediate corollary of exact count-law coverage and the defining confidence-set union, not an independent solve target. The exact \(m=1\), \(\epsilon=1/4\), uniform-count proposition is a sanity check. A complete boundary stratification and the exact \(m=2\) certificate remain open; growing or heterogeneous plate sizes belong to the two retained follow-on seeds rather than the present kernel.
